answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Main resource type for a Cosmos/DocumentDB account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources include databases and collections under that account).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Core CLI group: az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name <accountName> --resource-group <rg> --locations regionName='<region>' --kind MongoDB. MongoDB-specific subcommands are under az cosmosdb mongodb and az cosmosdb database/collection. This is part of the main azure-cli (not an extension).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: acctName ... }). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (example resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "..." location = "..." offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" }).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer:
Typical MongoDB API connection string for Cosmos DB: use mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. Non-SRV example (TLS port):
mongodb://<username>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&readPreference=secondaryPreferred&appName=@<account>@  
Username typically formatted as <dbuser>@<account>; password is the account primary key. The host suffix is *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and the TLS port commonly used is 10255. Important options: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false (Cosmos historically required this), and set a sane readPreference. For SRV you can use mongodb+srv://<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/ with TLS.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Cosmos/DocumentDB is billed in Request Units (RUs) provisioned per database/collection or at account level. There are manual RU/s (fixed), Autoscale RU (auto-scaling of RUs), and a serverless option for small/occasional workloads. It is not billed by vCores in the standard Cosmos DB model (RUs are the primary unit).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: For the MongoDB API the common authentication method is username/password (MongoDB SCRAM-style authentication) where the username includes the account and the password is one of the account keys. Connections must use TLS. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is not generally supported for the MongoDB wire-protocol endpoint — you authenticate with account keys/credentials. (If you need AAD for management plane operations use az login; but data-plane MongoDB drivers use the account credentials.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., npm package mongodb for Node.js). Do not use the Cosmos DB SQL (azure-cosmos) SDK when talking to the MongoDB wire protocol; use the MongoDB driver. There is a Cosmos SDK for the Core/SQL API, but for MongoDB compatibility you should use MongoDB drivers.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: As I understand Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API does not natively provide built-in vector indexes (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) like specialized vector DBs. There is no Cosmos-specific createVectorIndex command in the MongoDB API. If vector search is needed you would integrate with an external vector engine or use Azure Cognitive Search / custom service. (No native vector index creation command for Cosmos MongoDB API.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search is not a first-class built-in feature of Cosmos DB's MongoDB API. Typical approach is to index documents into Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) and run text or hybrid queries there, or use an external search service (Elastic, OpenSearch). Azure Cognitive Search can be connected to Cosmos DB via indexers or pushed indexing.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Historically Cosmos DB's MongoDB API has supported a limited subset of MongoDB server versions (common supported compatibility targets in the past were 3.6 and 4.0, newer accounts added support for later compatibility levels incrementally). Not all MongoDB features are supported: server-side JavaScript (db.eval), some aggregation operators, some admin commands, and certain storage-engine specific behaviors may be missing or behave differently. Multi-document transactions and some advanced features were only added later or are limited. Expect some incompatibilities between a genuine MongoDB server and Cosmos's MongoDB API.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is a Cosmos DB Emulator for the Cosmos SQL (Core) API; historically the emulator does NOT fully support the MongoDB API. For local development against a MongoDB-compatible interface use a local MongoDB server (Docker image mongo:latest) on the standard MongoDB port 27017. If you need to test Cosmos-specific behaviors you must test against a live Cosmos DB account (or the emulator where supported).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB exposes a change feed concept in the Core API. The MongoDB API historically did not provide full native MongoDB change streams in all compatibility versions; behavior differs. If you need document-change notifications you should use Cosmos DB change feed or the management/diagnostic tools that integrate with it. For MongoDB drivers, watch() support may be limited or unavailable depending on the compatibility version. No simple toggle to enable MongoDB-style change streams in older accounts.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile for data-plane inspection and tools specific to Cosmos/DocumentDB. The generic Azure MCP server (for Azure Resource Manager) covers provisioning and management but the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane helpers (indexes/collections/query plans) for this service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name for the service that was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB was the Core/SQL API). Azure Cosmos DB is Microsoft's globally distributed, multi-model database service. It is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB and also distinct from AWS DocumentDB (Amazon DocumentDB is an AWS service).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB uses Microsoft's proprietary storage and query engine; for the MongoDB API it implements the MongoDB wire protocol on top of its engine. Application code should use MongoDB drivers and standard MongoDB APIs but be aware of behavioral differences and unsupported MongoDB features (so some server-side features or admin commands may not work exactly like a native MongoDB server).

answers.question: What index definition does this sample need for composite unique deduplication on (customerId, eventId)?
answers.answer: Create a compound unique index on (customerId, eventId): db.events.createIndex({ customerId: 1, eventId: 1 }, { unique: true, name: 'customer_event_unique' })

answers.question: Which MongoDB API call should the Node.js ingestion service use for high-throughput unordered bulk writes?
answers.answer: Use collection.bulkWrite(operationsArray, { ordered: false }) from the official mongodb Node.js driver (or use bulk operations API like initializeUnorderedBulkOp() in older drivers). Example: await collection.bulkWrite(bulkOps, { ordered: false });

answers.question: How should the sample open a change stream to trigger downstream profile updates?
answers.answer: Use the MongoDB driver's change stream API: const changeStream = collection.watch(pipeline, { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); changeStream.on('change', doc => { /* enqueue profile update job */ }); Note: if the target Cosmos account does not support MongoDB-style change streams, use the Cosmos DB change feed mechanism instead.

answers.question: How must the sample read the connection string and connect (exact Node.js connection code and options)?
answers.answer: Read from env DOCUMENTDB_URI and connect with MongoClient using TLS and the unified topology. Example: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; const client = new MongoClient(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true }); await client.connect(); Use the sample DB name sample_customer_360_02 and do not log the URI.

answers.question: Which database and collection names and throughput expectations should the sample use/create?
answers.answer: Use database name sample_customer_360_02 and create a collection named events. Ensure the collection has adequate RU/s provisioned for bulk ingest (either provision RUs at collection level or rely on account autoscale); document the RU/s value in the run report. The sample will create the index and then run bulkWrite into sample_customer_360_02.events.
